Why do we need to redefine and create "new" words to describe situations where normal English would suffice? Is this a trend that has happened in other countries?
Is Politically Correct speech truly correct?

Well, it offends people (and is wrong) when someone refers to a black British person as "African American", and it offends others when you refer to someone as black. So, I don't think it's a game that can be won.

Being "politically correct" is a losing game: by doing so you're trying to offend as few people as possible, but being offended is ultimately one's own responsibility. Focusing on whether you might offend someone by saying something is just a distraction through which any real message is lost.

Sometimes. In the end, there's a thing. And then there's what you dress it up as, the way you present it to other people, all tidy and neat. And that's what political correctness is. The cleaned up, pretty version of a thing, which isn't necessarily an accurate reflection of what it truly is. It's not always truthful, but it's rarely a complete lie, either. It's not entirely wrong, but it's not the full reality either.

The reason we have politically correct terms to describe things we already have words for is for two reasons, I think. One is because people don't want to offend others for no reason. Certain ways of describing certain things, while truthful (from particular perspectives) are offensive unnecessarily. PC terms exist to describe the same thing without being unnecessarily offensive. The standard usage people have come to expect, however, is a sugar coat; it's not truthful at all, just hiding the truth behind a pleasant lie.

Another reason is because to an extent, PC phrasing can be more clinical. Instead of calling someone a foreigner, which depending on usage and who's saying it can be a derogatory term, you can say "person from another country". While the meaning would seem the same, it avoids the negative connotations of the other word. You say precisely what you want, without leaving very much room for people to misinterpret (or selective interpret) what you've said. Since politicians' words are frequently turned into weapons and used against them by their opponents, it's preferable to them to leave as little ambiguity as possible.
